text:
IN THE SUPREME
COURT OF BRITISH COLUMBIA

Citation:

Kau v. Triffo,

2007 BCSC 1851

Date: 20071221

Docket:
S054353

Registry: Vancouver

Between:

Larry Kau, Anthony D’Acquisto and
William S. Miller

Plaintiffs

And

Alexandra Triffo and S. Russel
Chamberlain

Defendants

And

Rakesh
Saxena

Third
Party

Before:
The Honourable Mr. Justice Cohen

Reasons for Judgment

(In Chambers)

Counsel for the plaintiffs

P.
Hildebrand

Counsel for the defendant S. Russel
Chamberlain

T.
Jespersen

Date and Place
of Hearing:

November 20, 2007

Vancouver, B.C.

THE APPLICATION

[
1
]

This is an application by the defendant S. Russel
Chamberlain (the “defendant”) for an order that the plaintiffs post security
for his costs of the action in the amount of $20,000, and that the action be
stayed until such security is posted.

BACKGROUND

[
2
]

The events leading up to the plaintiffs’ action
are mainly set out in the affidavits of the plaintiffs Larry Kau (“Kau”), sworn
August 27, 2007 and William Miller (“Miller”), sworn August 27, 2007 or
contained in the plaintiffs’ written submission in response to the defendant’s
application:

1.         The plaintiff Kau first met the defendant Alexandra
Triffo (“Triffo”) in the late 1990s.  Triffo was a Vancouver stock broker, who
executed some trades on Kau’s behalf.

2.         In the spring of 1999, Triffo traveled to Wisconsin and
advised Kau that she was promoting a company called Global Explorations Corp.
(“GEC”), a public company whose shares traded on the TSX Venture Exchange and
through the “Pink Sheets”.  Triffo gave Kau some promotional materials
concerning GEC.  Kau noted from those materials that the Third Party Rakesh
Saxena (“Saxena”) was President of GEC.  Kau did not know Saxena.

3.         A few months later, in June 1999, Triffo called Kau again
and advised him that there was a substantial block of GEC stock available for
sale by way of private sale at a discounted price of US$0.33 per share.  Triffo
also advised that:

(a)       funds for the purchase of GEC stock should be sent to the
defendant, in trust; and

(b)       the stock which was to be purchased was being held by the
defendant in escrow, to be delivered against payment, with the result that the
transaction was safe for Kau, in the sense that he was certain to receive any
shares he paid for.

Triffo also
advised Kau that the transaction would have to proceed quickly.

4.         None of the plaintiffs knew who was the actual owner of
the stock they were purchasing, though Kau understood from Triffo that the
proceeds would be used to repay a loan made to GEC by a Mr. Hammond.  It turns
out that:

(a)       the vendor was Saxena; and

(b)       the defendant was Saxena’s lawyer, representing him in
extradition proceedings brought by Thailand in respect of alleged fraudulent
banking activities there.  At the time, Saxena was under house arrest in Canada
while the extradition proceedings were pending.

The plaintiffs
did not know that Saxena was a client of the defendant (and Miller, in
particular, did not even know Saxena’s name).

5.         Kau contacted two of his business acquaintances, the
plaintiff Anthony D’Acquisto (“D’Acquisto”) and Miller, who also decided to
purchase part of the stock.  Kau is a construction worker by trade, D’Acquisto
runs a fruit importing business in Milwaukee, and Miller is a semi-retired
advertising executive.

6.         Each of the plaintiffs provided funds for the purchase,
which ended up in the defendant’s trust account by diverse means:

(a)       Kau had his brokerage firm in Vancouver deliver a $16,000
cheque, payable to the defendant in trust, to Triffo.  Kau was also hoping to
borrow additional funds to buy more stock, so he also sent Triffo a signed
personal cheque, with the amount left blank, also payable to the defendant in
trust.  Without Kau’s authority, Triffo filled in an amount of US$100,000 in
the personal cheque.  Both cheques were caused to be delivered to the defendant
by Saxena.  The defendant received the US$100,000 cheque first, but it was
returned NSF.  He subsequently received the $16,000 cheque, which was deposited
into his trust account.

(b)       D’Acquisto wire transferred US$75,240 (part of which
represented a loan to Kau) to the defendant’s trust account.

(c)        Miller obtained a US bank draft for US$25,000, and sent
it by courier to Triffo.  Triffo apparently gave it to Saxena, who gave it to the
defendant.  The bank draft had noted expressly on it “for Seventy Five Thousand
Shares of Global Explorations stock”.

7.         Kau and Miller never received any of their stock.
Approximately two years after the events in question, and after D’Acquisto and
Kau had expressed considerable anger to Triffo, D’Acquisto received from Triffo
a share certificate for 96,500 shares in Global Explorations, Inc. (a successor
company to GEC), registered in the name of Oceanwest Landscaping Ltd., a
company apparently owned by Triffo.  D’Acquisto was not able to make any use of
the share certificate, as it was not registered in his name.  Several years
following the transaction, D’Acquisto also received a share certificate of
Global Explorations, Inc. representing 45,000 shares registered in his name.
By that time, however, the shares were worthless.

8.         Kau and Miller depose expressly that the plaintiffs did
not at any time authorize the defendant to pay the funds in question to Saxena,
or assign or transfer any beneficial interest in those funds to Saxena.

9.         In the summer of 2005, the plaintiffs commenced an action
against Triffo and the defendant in Wisconsin.  Shortly afterwards, they
commenced this proceeding in British Columbia.  The British Columbia proceeding
was not served – it was commenced only as a backup, in case the defendant was
able to resist jurisdiction in Wisconsin successfully.

10.       In March 2006, the Wisconsin proceedings were dismissed.
This proceeding was served subsequently.

11.       The plaintiffs say that they do not know what ultimately
happened to their funds.  They presume they were used to pay legal bills owing
by Saxena to the defendant, or they may have been disbursed out of the
defendant’s trust account to or for the benefit of Saxena.  The parties have
exchanged lists of documents, but the defendant’s list has only one entry:

Copies of pleadings
and proceedings in the United States District Court Eastern District of
Wisconsin between Anthony D’Acquisto, Larry Kau and William S. Miller,
Plaintiffs and Alexandra Triffo and S. Russel Chamberlain, Defendants, Case No.
05-C-0810.

12.       Oral discoveries have not been conducted.  A trial date is
set for March 2008.

THE
DEFENDANT’S POSITION

[
3
]

In his statement of defence filed December 22,
2006, the defendant pleads,
inter alia
, as follows:

In further answer to the allegations contained
in the Statement of Claim, This Defendant says, and the facts are, the funds
referred to in the Statement of Claim (the “Funds”) were paid to him on the
instructions, or at the direction of Rakesh Saxena (“Saxena”) who, at all
material times, represented to This Defendant that he had the express and/or
implied authority of the Plaintiffs to deposit the Funds and to thereafter
provide instructions with respect to their disbursement.

In the alternative and in further answer to the
allegations contained in the Statement of Claim, This Defendant says that with
respect to the Funds referred to in paragraphs 7(b) and 7(c) of the Statement
of Claim that the Plaintiffs, Kau and D’Acquisto confirmed they placed no
conditions on This Defendant with respect to those funds.  In doing so, This Defendant
says and the facts are that the Plaintiffs Kau and D’Acquisto, by their
conduct, were confirming that Saxena had actual or ostensible authority to
provide instructions with respect to those funds to This Defendant.

In further answer to the allegations contained
in the Statement of Claim, This Defendant says that the Plaintiffs, and each of
them, in the circumstances, clothed Saxena with actual and/or apparent or
ostensible authority over the disposition of the Funds and This Defendant was
entitled, at all material times, to disburse the Funds in accordance with
Saxena’s instructions.

In the alternative and in further answer to the
allegations contained in the Statement of Claim, This Defendant says that the
plaintiff Miller clothed the Plaintiff Kau with actual and/or apparent or
ostensible authority over the disposition of the funds he provided and This Defendant
was entitled, at all material times, to disburse those funds in accordance with
Kau’s and/or Saxena’s instructions.

[
4
]

In his affidavit sworn October 4, 2005, in
support of his motion to dismiss the proceedings in the United States District
Court Eastern District of Wisconsin, the defendant deposed,
inter alia
,
as follows:

At no time up until I received a telephone call
on January 29, 2001 from Larry Kau, was I aware of any of the complaints or
problems alluded to by the Plaintiffs herein.

I was not privy, party or knowledgeable with
respect to the transaction between the Plaintiffs on the one hand and Alexandra
Triffo on the other.  I had no communications directly or indirectly with
Alexandra Triffo until as set out in this, my Affidavit, namely February 1
2001.  I was never asked by anyone, including the Plaintiffs, to hold funds “in
trust” pending the delivery of shares and indeed I did not know the funds were
delivered to the benefit of Rakesh Saxena for the purposes of purchasing shares
if indeed they were.

When funds are made payable to my law firm,
whether they are marked “in trust” or otherwise, the funds always go into a
pooled trust account unless they are to pay directly an account rendered by me
or my law firm.

I had no interest, directly or indirectly in
any manner whatsoever in Global Explorations Corporation stock nor did I
facilitate the transfer, the delivery or the conveyance in any way whatsoever
of that stock to the Plaintiffs herein.

I did not have any contact direct or indirect
by any means whatsoever with the Plaintiffs herein prior to the deposit of the
funds and the first contact with any of the Plaintiffs was by telephone as set
out in paragraph 25 of this, my Affidavit.

No trust relationship was ever imposed upon me
by the Plaintiffs and I never accepted a trust relationship with the Plaintiffs.

[
5
]

The defendant’s basis for seeking the order is
that none of the plaintiffs reside in British Columbia; none of them own
exigible property in British Columbia; there are meritorious defences to the
claim; the defendant will incur significant expenses in defending the claim
(the defendant has drafted a bill of costs that totals $35,000); and all of the
plaintiffs reside in the state of Wisconsin, which is not a reciprocating state
pursuant to the
Court Order Enforcement Act
, R.S.B.C. 1996, c. 78
(the “
Act
”).

[
6
]

In support of his application, the defendant
relies upon the principles summarized in
Kropp v. Swaneset Bay Golf
Course Ltd.
,
1997 CanLII 4037 (BC CA)
, 29 B.C.L.R. (3d) 252, [1997] 4 W.W.R. 306 (C.A.) at para.

17
:

1.         The
court has a complete discretion whether to order security, and will act in
light of all the relevant circumstances;

2.         The
possibility or probability that the plaintiff company will be deterred from
pursuing its claim is not without more sufficient reason for not ordering
security;

3.         The
court must attempt to balance injustices arising from use of security as an
instrument of oppression to stifle a legitimate claim on the one hand, and use
of impecuniosity as a means of putting unfair pressure on a defendant on the
other;

4.         The
court may have regard to the merits of the action, but should avoid going into
detail on the merits unless success or failure appears obvious;

5.         The
court can order any amount of security up to the full amount claimed, as long
as the amount is more than nominal;

6.         Before
the court refuses to order security on the ground that it would unfairly stifle
a valid claim, the court must be satisfied that, in all the circumstances, it
is probable that the claim would be stifled; and

7.         The
lateness of the application for security is a circumstance which can properly
be taken into account.

[
7
]

As well, Romilly J. in
Citizens for
Foreign Aid Reform Inc. v. Canadian Jewish Congress
,
1999 CanLII 5860 (BC SC)
, 36 C.P.C. (4
th
)
266, [1999] B.C.J. No. 2160 (S.C.) (QL) set out the following test at para. 14:

Based then, on the decision in
Kropp
, supra

as well as the decision of Spencer J. in
Ruko, supra,
the test to be
applied on an application for security for costs is as follows:

1.         Does
it appear that the plaintiff company will be unable to pay the defendants’
costs if the action fails?

2.         If
so, has the plaintiff shown that it has exigible assets of sufficient value to
satisfy an award of costs?

3.         Is
the court satisfied that the defendants have an arguable defence to present?

4.         Would
an order for costs visit undue hardship on the plaintiff such that it would
prevent the plaintiff’s case from being heard?

[
8
]

At para. 18, Romilly J. states that if a
defendant has shown a
prima facie
case that the plaintiff may be unable
to pay costs, the plaintiff may avoid an order for security by showing that it
has exigible assets.  At para. 23, His Lordship states:

In sum, on an application for security for
costs, once the defendants have established a prima facie case that the
plaintiff lacks exigible assets, the plaintiff is required to respond with
evidence to establish either that it will be able to pay the defendants’ costs,
that the defendants have no arguable case, or that an order for security will
stifle the action.  These tests serve to balance the possible injustice of
stifling the corporate plaintiff’s claim against the possible injustices of
exposing the defendants to a law suit where they could not recover their costs
if successful.

[
9
]

The defence says that as the defendant has
established a meritorious defence; that the plaintiffs do not reside in a
reciprocating state; and that the plaintiffs lack exigible assets in the
jurisdiction, accordingly, the court should grant the order sought.

THE PLAINTIFFS’ POSITION

[
10
]

The plaintiffs concede that they do not reside
in the jurisdiction; that they have no exigible assets in the jurisdiction; and
that they reside in a non-reciprocating jurisdiction.  As well, they do not
allege impecuniosity.

[
11
]

The main point relied upon to defeat the
defendant’s application is that the application for security for costs against an
individual plaintiff is considered differently from a corporate plaintiff.  In
Higgins
v. Willis
,
2003 BCSC 1850
, 45 C.P.C. (5
th
) 246, Barrow J.
states at para. 7, as follows:

The court has the inherent jurisdiction to
order security for costs against an individual (
Tordoff v. Canada Life
Assurance Co.,
1985 CanLII 492 (BC SC)
, [1985] B.C.J. No. 2800 (S.C.) at para.
14
).  It is a
jurisdiction that is to be used “with great caution” (
Gray v. Powerassist
Tehnologies Inc.
,
2001 BCSC 1208 (CanLII)
, [2001] B.C.J. No. 1722 (S.C.) at para.
20
).  It is only
to be invoked “sparingly” (
Tordoff
,
at para.
14
).  The jurisdiction to
award security for costs against a corporate party is found in
s. 205
of the
Company
Act
, R.S.B.C. 1996, c. 62.  The discretion conferred on the court by that
section is broader than the discretion the court has to order security for
costs in relation to individuals.  The reason for this distinction flows from
the rationale for the rule as it relates to corporations.  As Joyce J. put it
in
Gray
at para.
20
:

The rationale behind
the statutory provision concerning corporations is to provide protection to
defendants from abuse by natural persons funding litigation brought by
impecunious corporations, while standing behind the corporate veil and taking
the benefit of impunity from any personal liability for costs.  That rationale
is not present in the case of the individual plaintiff.  He is exposed to an
order for costs.  In the English case of
Pearson v. Naydler
,
[1977] 3
All E.R. 531 (Ch. Div.)
, referred to in
Kropp v. Swaneset Bay Golf Course
Ltd.
,
supra,
Vice Chancellor Megarry said at p. 533:

The basic rule that
a natural person who sues will not be ordered to give security for costs,
however poor he is, is ancient and well-established.  As Bowen LJ said in
Cowell
v. Taylor
[
(1885), 31 Ch.D. 34 at 38
], both at law and in equity ‘the
general rule is that poverty is no bar to a litigant’.  The power to require
security for costs ought not to be used so as to bar even the poorest man from
the courts.

[
12
]

The plaintiffs also rely on
Tordoff
v.
Canada Life Assurance Company
(1985),
1985 CanLII 492 (BC SC)
, 64 B.C.L.R. 46, a decision where
the court held that an individual plaintiff should post security for future
costs.  On p. 50 Proudfoot J. (as she then was) states, as follows:

I am satisfied the court does have the inherent jurisdiction to make
an order in some cases.  The power would have to be exercised cautiously,
sparingly and indeed
under very special circumstances
.

[emphasis
mine]

[
13
]

The plaintiffs argue that the authorities relied
upon by the defendant reflect the distinction and cannot support the order
sought in this case.  They point out that most of the authorities cited by the
defence are ones involving corporate claims, or they are cases where the claims
of individuals were closely connected to the corporate claims, or they were
claims involving highly unique circumstances adverse to the plaintiff: See
Beasse
v. Holness
,
2006 BCSC 1265
, [2006] B.C.J. No. 1928 (QL);
Fat
Mel’s Restaurant Ltd. v. Canadian Northern Shield Insurance Co.
(1993),

1993 CanLII 1669 (BC CA)
, 76 B.C.L.R. (2d) 231, 25 B.C.A.C. 95 (C.A.);
Kropp v. Swaneset Bay Golf
Course Ltd.
,
supra
;
Citizens for Foreign Aid Reform Inc.
v. Canadian Jewish Congress
,
supra
.

DECISION

[
14
]

I agree with the plaintiffs’ position that in
considering whether to exercise discretion to make an order, the courts draw a
distinction between corporate and individual plaintiffs, and treat corporate
plaintiffs with less generosity and flexibility than they do individual
plaintiffs: See
Fat Mel’s Restaurant Ltd.,
supra
, at para.
27.  As the authorities provide, in cases where the court is asked to order
security for costs against an individual, the court tends to exercise its
discretion more cautiously.  Examples can be found where the court determined
that there were special circumstances to support the grant of such an order
against an individual plaintiff.

[
15
]

In
Dick v. Vancouver City Savings Credit
Union
,
2006 BCSC 810
, [2006] B.C.J. No. 1215, the court commented that
on a review of the pleadings, while the statement of claim alleged fraud,
discrimination, conspiracy and fraudulent and negligent misrepresentation
against the defendants, it appeared on a plain reading of the statement of
claim that the principal problem was the plaintiff’s lack of financing for the various
developments, and failure to attend and defend foreclosure proceedings.  The
defendants therefore saw lengthy and protracted proceedings, given the
prolixity of the pleadings and the fact that the plaintiff was self-represented,
without any prospect of recovering their costs.  Considering the circumstances,
the court ordered that security for costs be posted by the individual
plaintiff.

[
16
]

In
Tordoff
, supra
, the
plaintiff claimed that he had been injured in a motor vehicle accident and
started an action against I.C.B.C. and against the insurer who covered him
under a group disability policy.  Both insurers denied that any accident had
occurred.  At p. 52, Proudfoot J. outlined the circumstances that satisfied her
that she should order security for costs against an individual plaintiff:

Finally, the plaintiff’s credibility has
already suffered considerably.  The inconsistencies are many and major,
cross-examination has not been concluded by counsel for the Canada Life
Assurance Company, and he has yet to be cross-examined by counsel for the Insurance
Corporation of British Columbia.  It is a fair assessment from the evidence to
this point that the plaintiff’s case has many problems.

I think it is also fair to conclude at this
stage, in all the circumstances, that even if the plaintiff succeeds in his
claim, he has a good deal of difficulty in establishing anything other than a
limited claim for a minor injury.  The Godfrey report makes a comparison that
if the accident occurred, it is to be compared to that of “heavy braking”.

Finally, I note the following.  The plaintiff
indicated at the time of the trial that he would be commencing a new job in
1984.  He was not gainfully employed during the trial and apparently is not
employed at this stage.  The material filed by the plaintiff is totally silent
on the plaintiff’s present activities.  The home where the plaintiff resides,
with a Ms. Hooker, is owned by her.  The plaintiff admitted during the course
of his cross-examination that he had not paid a maintenance order to support
his children and was indeed being sought by the Provincial Court to enforce
that order.  It seems that he had left the jurisdiction and returned to Britain
to avoid payment.  There certainly is no doubt that the position by the
defendants is accurate that, if the defendants are successful, they most
certainly will not be successful in recovering any costs for this protracted
trial.

[
17
]

On the other hand, in
Ng and Tang v. Royal
& Sun Alliance Insurance Co.

2000 BCSC 1683
, 24 C.C.L.I. (3d) 71,
R.R. Holmes J. dismissed an application for security for costs against
individual plaintiffs.  In that case, the plaintiffs had no assets in B.C., but
claimed a base of substantial wealth in Hong Kong and Mainland China.  The court
noted that Hong Kong is not a reciprocating state under the
Court Order
Enforcement Act
.  The court also noted that on the evidence the
plaintiffs had very substantial assets, but none remained within the court’s
jurisdiction.  After an assessment of the circumstances and application of the
legal principles, the court said at para. 26 that a very strong factor was the
absence of any suggestion that a recovery in Hong Kong could not be made by the
usual process of suit upon a judgment of the court and then went on to state:

There appears no possibility here that the
defendant would ever experience a “dry judgment” which, in the end result, is
the primary basis of the Court in considering a requirement for posting of
security.

[
18
]

In the instant case, essentially all that the
defence has established is that the plaintiffs are non-residents and have no
exigible property in this jurisdiction.  The law is well settled that these
factors are not enough to make the order sought:
Sheill v. Coach House
Hotel Ltd.
(1982),
1982 CanLII 454 (BC CA)
, 37 B.C.L.R. 254 at p. 260, 136 D.L.R. (3d) 470
(C.A.)

[
19
]

Moreover, in my opinion, the defendant has
failed to establish the existence of special circumstances.  There is no proof
that if the defendant succeeds in his defence to the claims that he will not be
able to recover his costs from the plaintiffs.

[
20
]

Keeping in mind the law that an order for
security for costs against an individual plaintiff should be granted with
caution and used sparingly, I find that in the circumstances before the court
the defendant’s application must be dismissed.

“B.I. Cohen J.”

|The Honourable Mr. Justice B.I. Cohen
